Panpsychism. The philosophical view that consciousness or some form of experience is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world—not confined to human brains or even biological systems, but present in all matter to some degree. Rather than treating consciousness as an anomalous emergent property that somehow arises from non-conscious matter, panpsychism suggests that mentality is woven into reality at the most basic level. It offers a radical response to the mind-body problem and the explanatory gap between physical processes and subjective experience.

Panpsychism proposes that consciousness is fundamental, not emergent—a basic feature of reality like mass or charge. It avoids both dualism, the implausible split between mind and matter, and the apparent inadequacy of standard materialism to explain subjective experience.

The view takes seriously the puzzle of qualia: how do objective physical processes give rise to subjective, qualitative feelings? It has ancient roots in Spinoza and Leibniz and has been revived in contemporary philosophy of mind by thinkers like Galen Strawson.

Panpsychism addresses the combination problem: if electrons have micro-experiences, how do they combine into the unified, large-scale consciousness we enjoy? This raises hard questions. Does an electron have experience? If so, how does individual consciousness arise from billions of micro-experiences?

The view contrasts with emergence theories that treat consciousness as a novel, non-reducible phenomenon arising only at higher levels of complexity. Constitutive panpsychism argues consciousness constitutes or grounds physical properties rather than vice versa.

Cosmopsychism extends the view further: the universe itself, not just its parts, is conscious or experiences as a unified whole. Panpsychism motivates alternative frameworks and offers a solution to the hard problem by reconceptualizing consciousness as part of nature's fundamental architecture.

Panpsychism connects to consciousness, reconceived as universal rather than rare and special. It offers a novel solution to the ancient mind-body problem of how mind relates to matter. It avoids dualism's problems by denying the hard separation between mind and physical reality. It challenges standard materialism's claim that consciousness emerges from wholly non-conscious processes. It directly addresses the hard problem of explaining subjective experience through panpsychic unity. It is central to contemporary philosophy of mind. And it represents a major rethinking of fundamental categories in ontology.
